Meta.title: Brazil Election Gauge — political risk in Brazilian stock prices
Meta.description: Quantitative dashboard of the largest B3 companies: Sharpe, volatility, beta, multiples, historical election sensitivity, and a post-2026 scenario simulator.

Footer.howToReadBody: Everything here measures the past. Betas, Sharpe ratios, and election sensitivity describe how these stocks behaved — not how they will behave. History itself shows the limits: in 2014 the market spent months pricing an alternation that never came, and in 2022 the election barely moved prices while the damage showed up later, during the transition.
Footer.dataBody: Prices: {prices}. Macro: {macro}. Tesouro Direto: official rates from Tesouro Transparente. Series since 2013, updated on {updated}. Run <command>npm run fetch-data</command> to fetch fresh quotes.
Footer.disclaimer: Informational and educational content only. Not investment advice, securities analysis, or an offer to buy or sell.

MacroHeader.title: Brazil Election Gauge
MacroHeader.description: How much of the price of Brazil's largest B3 companies is political risk — and how much is everything else. Metrics computed from real price history since 2013, with a study of the 2014, 2018, and 2022 elections.

risco.label: Risk and return
risco.description: How each stock behaved over the last 3 years, always compared with the CDI — the real alternative for anyone investing in Brazil.

valuation.label: Price and fundamentals
valuation.description: What you pay for each stock: multiples, dividends, and the gap between today's price and the median of the last 3 years.

politica.label: Politics and rates
politica.description: How far each stock diverges from the Ibovespa in election season and how it has historically reacted to Selic moves.

sectorHints.bancos: Sorted by P/B. Below 1, the market pays less than book value — the discount on Banco do Brasil and the regionals is structural, not an automatic mispricing.
sectorHints.energia: Listed utilities: generation, transmission, and distribution. Low P/B shows up in transmission (ISA, Alupar) and Cemig; Equatorial and Eneva trade at a growth multiple.
sectorHints.baratas: Only names trading below book value. Compare with the 3-year median: a low multiple after a rally can still be expensive versus its own history.

RankingTable.footer: Click any row to open the full company analysis. Hover a column name to see how the metric is calculated.
RankingTable.bananaTooltip: P/B {pb} — below book value. That is a discount, not a guarantee of upside.

cagr3y.label: Return p.a. (3y)
cagr3y.help: Annualized total return over the last 3 years, including reinvested dividends.

excessOverCdi.label: vs CDI
excessOverCdi.help: How much the stock returned above (or below) the CDI over the same period, annualized. Negative means fixed income would have been better.

vol.label: Volatility
vol.help: Annualized standard deviation of daily returns. Higher means the price swings more.

sharpe.label: Sharpe
sharpe.help: Return above the CDI divided by volatility. Measures how much extra return you got per unit of risk. Negative: you took risk and still lost to fixed income.

beta.label: Beta
beta.help: Sensitivity to the Ibovespa. A beta of 1.5 means the stock tends to rise or fall 1.5% when the index moves 1%.

dd.label: Max drawdown
dd.help: The largest peak-to-trough drop within the last 3 years. The size of the pain the history has already delivered.

vsMedian.label: vs 3y median
vsMedian.help: Today's price versus the median of the last 3 years — the 'typical price'. The marker shows where the stock sits in its historical distribution.

vsHigh.label: vs 52w high
vsHigh.help: Distance to the high of the last 12 months.

pe.label: P/E
pe.help: Price divided by trailing twelve-month earnings. How many years of current profit you pay for the company.

pb.label: P/B
pb.help: Price to book. Below 1 means the market pays less than the company's accounting equity.

dy.label: Dividends 12m
dy.help: Distributions paid over the last 12 months over the current price. Compare with the CDI before calling it 'income'.

roe.label: ROE
roe.help: Return on equity: how much profit the company earns on shareholders' capital.

electionSensitivity.label: Election sensitivity
electionSensitivity.help: How far the stock diverges from the Ibovespa in election season, divided by how far it diverges the rest of the time. Above 1.00: the election really moves this stock beyond what it does to the index.

selicBeta.label: Selic +1 pp effect
selicBeta.help: Excess return versus the Ibovespa historically associated with each percentage point rise in the Selic. Negative values point to stocks that suffer when rates rise and benefit from cuts.

hiking.label: In hiking cycle
hiking.help: Annualized excess return versus the Ibovespa during periods when the Selic was rising.

easing.label: In easing cycle
easing.help: Annualized excess return versus the Ibovespa during periods when the Selic was falling.

usdBeta.label: USD beta
usdBeta.help: Effect of a stronger dollar on the stock, after stripping out what the Ibovespa explains. Positive indicates FX protection.

brentBeta.label: Oil beta
brentBeta.help: Effect of a Brent rally on the stock, after stripping out what the Ibovespa explains.

sections.electionHistory: Election history · excess return vs Ibovespa

AssetDetail.factorsNote: USD, Brent, and Treasury enter after stripping out the Ibovespa effect, so they measure what remains beyond the index move. The model explains {rSquared} of the stock's daily variation across {observations} sessions.
AssetDetail.noElectionHistory: No trading history covering prior elections.

PriceDistribution.title: Where today's price sits within the last 3 years
PriceDistribution.intro: The arithmetic mean lies when the series has spikes and collapses: a short rally is enough to pull the whole number. That is why the reference here is the median and the quartiles. The bar shows the range from the period low to the high, the darker band holds the middle half of sessions, and the marker is the current price.
PriceDistribution.footer: Being below the median does not mean cheap, and being above does not mean expensive. A company whose earnings doubled deserves to trade above its own history; another in decline can fall forever. The percentile says where the price is, not whether the price makes sense.

ElectionStudy.title: What each stock did in excess of the Ibovespa
ElectionStudy.intro: Every figure nets out the index move. What shows up in the table is company-specific — the political premium or discount the market assigned to it, not the tide that lifted or sank every boat.
ElectionStudy.footnote: The most useful reading is not the next-day column, but comparing the prior 90 sessions with the year after. When a stock rallies hard beforehand and gives it back later, the market bought the expectation and sold the fact.

2014.pricedIn: Alternation rally: the market rose hard from March to September as polls suggested a change of government.
2014.note: The limiting case of an election priced in too early. The reversal came on election night, and state-controlled names gave back the premium they had built up.

2018.pricedIn: A liberal agenda with Paulo Guedes at Finance, privatization promises, and pension reform.
2018.note: The result confirmed the scenario the market had been buying since September, so the rally came before — and continued after.

2022.pricedIn: A Lula win widely expected in the polls, with doubt about the new term's fiscal anchor.
2022.note: The election itself barely moved prices. The damage came later, with the Transition PEC — showing that what matters is what the government does, not who wins.

pre90.label: 90 sessions before
pre90.description: The election race itself. This is where the market recalculates probabilities and moves prices.

d1.label: 1st session after 1st round
d1.description: The immediate reaction to the result. Measures how surprised the market was.

d5.label: 5 sessions after 1st round
d5.description: The first week, after the initial shock noise fades.

runoffD1.label: 1st session after runoff
runoffD1.description: The reaction to the definitive winner.

post60.label: 60 sessions after runoff
post60.description: The government transition: economic team, early fiscal signals.

post250.label: 1 year after runoff
post250.description: The real test. Election euphoria either becomes a structural rally — or evaporates.

ScenarioSimulator.chooseIntro: Each scenario is a set of shocks over a 6-month horizon. Adjust the controls to build your own.
ScenarioSimulator.resultsIntro: Projection built from each stock's historical betas. A sensitivity reading, not a forecast: it shows how these companies tended to react to similar shocks.

ibov.label: Ibovespa
ibov.help: The move of the market as a whole.

selic.label: Selic
selic.help: Change in the policy rate, in percentage points.

usdbrl.label: Dollar
usdbrl.help: An increase means a weaker real.

brent.label: Brent crude
brent.help: Commodity price on the international market.

ust10y.label: 10-year Treasury
ust10y.help: US long rates: a rise tends to drain capital from emerging markets.

neutral.name: Nothing changes
neutral.summary: The election confirms what was already in the price. Rates, FX, and oil stay put. Serves as a baseline to compare everything else against.

promarket.name: Pro-market turn
promarket.summary: Outcome read as favorable to fiscal discipline and privatizations. The real strengthens, the yield curve rallies, and Copom can cut the Selic.

fiscalanchor.name: Continuity with a fiscal anchor
fiscalanchor.summary: The elected government presents a fiscal plan the market finds credible. The rally is smaller than in a full turn, but the rates channel works the same way.

fiscaldrift.name: No fiscal anchor
fiscaldrift.summary: Public spending accelerates, debt worsens, and the market demands a premium. The real weakens and the central bank starts hiking again.

oilshock.name: Oil shock
oilshock.summary: Brent spikes on geopolitical tension. Good for producers, bad for inflation — and reopens the debate over Petrobras pricing policy.

riskoff.name: Global risk-off
riskoff.summary: The problem comes from abroad: US long rates rise, the dollar strengthens, and foreign capital leaves emerging markets. The election becomes a sideshow.

directAnswer.title: Not automatically. Locking in IPCA+ today hedges inflation — not a Selic cut.
directAnswer.body1: Tesouro IPCA+ 2029 pays IPCA + {ipcaRate} real. With trailing 12-month IPCA at {ipca12m}, that is about {nominal} a year — less than CDI at {cdi}. Prefixed 2029 at {prefixRate} only loses to IPCA+ if average inflation through 2029 stays above {breakeven}. Below that, locking the prefixed bond today wins.
directAnswer.body2: IPCA+ stops being “40% of nothing” when Selic falls: the {midRate} real yield stays locked. CDI does not. But if Selic falls <emphasis>because</emphasis> inflation was brought under control, the prefixed bond — not IPCA+ — is the contract that gains most from buying now.

selic.title: Tesouro Selic / CDB
selic.body: Pays while Selic is high. The day rates fall, the yield falls with them. It is the only one that does not take a mark-to-market hit if you need the cash tomorrow.

prefixado.title: Tesouro Prefixed
prefixado.body: Wins if inflation cooperates and Selic falls. It is the bet on a fiscal anchor: Brazil conquers inflation and you kept 14% in the contract.

ipca.title: Tesouro IPCA+
ipca.body: Wins if inflation surprises to the upside. Today’s real yield is high by historical standards — locking in now makes sense for anyone who can hold to maturity.

scenarios.title: What if Selic and IPCA turn out differently?
scenarios.intro: The four scenarios below reprice bonds you would buy today, held to maturity, with regressive income tax. Nothing here is mark-to-market: it assumes you do not sell along the way.
scenarios.breakevenNote: Breakeven inflation for prefixed 2029 vs IPCA+ 2029: {breakeven}. Above that, IPCA+ beats the prefixed bond.
scenarios.bestNet: Best after-tax net in this scenario
scenarios.winnerLine: {net} net per year · {real} real after inflation
scenarios.cdbNote: The violet line is a CDB at 140% of CDI — the product from the original conversation. It shows up at mid-sized banks, with a locked term and FGC coverage. It is excluded from the winner pick because it is not comparable to Tesouro on liquidity or availability.

hoje.name: Rates as they are
hoje.summary: Selic stays at 14% and IPCA near the trailing 4.2%. This is the scenario where CDI keeps paying more than IPCA+ in nominal terms.

corte.name: Post-election cut
corte.summary: Credible fiscal plan, inflation anchored, Copom cuts Selic to 10%. CDI’s real yield falls; the IPCA+ real yield you already locked stays put.

desancora.name: No fiscal anchor
desancora.summary: Spending rises, inflation returns to 7% and Selic goes to 18%. Nominal CDI soars, but purchasing power is eaten. Anyone who locked IPCA+ at 7.5% real keeps what the prefixed bond loses.

meta.name: Inflation on target
meta.summary: IPCA at 3% — the central bank target — and Selic at 9%. CDI’s real yield shrinks; IPCA+ bought today at 7.5% real becomes an expensive contract to have walked away from.

history.title: What IPCA+ 2035 actually returned
history.intro: Buying IPCA+ is not the same as holding to maturity. The table below uses the market price of Tesouro IPCA+ 2035: the return of someone who sold midway. Over the last 3 years the real yield went from {fromRate} to {toRate}, and mark-to-market ate the coupon.
history.footer: Over 3 years CDI returned {cdi} a year. Anyone who bought IPCA+ 2035 and sold now got {sold} — losing to liquid fixed income and to equities. Anyone who holds to 2035 still receives the real yield locked at purchase. The difference between those two sentences is the holding period.

chart.title: Tesouro IPCA+ 2035 real yield · {rate} today
chart.intro: Each point on this chart is the real rate Tesouro was willing to lock that day. Buying IPCA+ in 2019 at 3.4% locked in cheap. Buying now near 7.5% is expensive for Tesouro and cheap for you — as long as you can avoid selling if the real yield goes to 8.5%.

menu.title: Current Tesouro Direto menu
menu.intro: Morning buy rates as of {date}. Implied nominal for IPCA+ uses trailing 12-month IPCA only as illustration — future inflation is what decides. Selic looks almost identical to CDI because the premium on those bonds is near zero.

thesis.PETR4: The federal government controls the vote. Fuel prices, investment pace, and dividend policy shift with whoever is in power — and that shows up in the multiple before it shows up in earnings.
thesis.BBAS3: Trades at a structural discount to private banks on political-balance-sheet risk (directed credit, farm subsidies). A government seen as capital-discipline friendly compresses that discount.
thesis.CMIG4: Controlled by Minas Gerais state. Every election cycle reopens privatization, dividends, and using the company as a fiscal tool for the state.
thesis.AXIA3: The former Eletrobras, renamed. Privatized, but with an open fight over the federal government’s voting power. The electric name where the election thesis is still more legal than operational.
thesis.CPLE3: Privatized Paraná utility. Generation, transmission, and distribution in one group: the multiple reacts to tariffs, hydrology, and the discount the market still charges for its state origins.
thesis.EQTL3: Distributor that grows by buying hard concessions and cutting losses and delinquency. An execution thesis, not a Brasília thesis.
thesis.ENGI11: Same model as Equatorial: distribution in high-loss regions, leveraged to operating improvement and the rate cycle.
thesis.CPFE3: Controlled by State Grid. Distribution and generation with more predictable cash flow than state-owned peers — the price follows rates and tariffs, not election polls.
thesis.EGIE3: Contracted generation controlled by France’s Engie. An income profile: what moves it is the real rate, because the dividend competes with Tesouro IPCA+.
thesis.ENEV3: Gas-fired thermal generation. Not Copel’s power bill: results depend on dispatch, gas, and contracts — more commodity than tariff.
thesis.ALUP11: Transmission in Brazil and Peru. Contracted revenue, inflation in the contract: the direct competitor is Tesouro IPCA+, not the Ibovespa.
thesis.ISAE4: Transmission (ex-Transmissão Paulista). Same logic as Taesa: high rates compress the multiple even with a stable contract.
thesis.AURE3: Renewable generation spun out of Votorantim. Still trades like a company being built: a low price can be an execution discount, not a margin of safety.
thesis.SBSP3: Privatized under a state government. Tariffs and the sanitation framework depend on regulation, so political risk is real — but state and regulatory, not federal.
thesis.B3SA3: Earns on traded volume. The purest way to bet on falling rates: a lower Selic pushes investors from fixed income into equities, and B3 takes a toll on every trade.
thesis.ITUB4: Exposed to the credit cycle and Selic, without the state bank’s political discount. Reacts to elections through macro (rates, defaults), not through ownership control.
thesis.BBDC4: Same logic as Itaú, with a book historically more sensitive to defaults — which amplifies a rate-cycle move.
thesis.SANB11: Controlled by Spain’s Santander. The discount vs Itaú usually comes from profitability, not political risk — so cheap here is an execution thesis, not an election one.
thesis.BRSR6: Rio Grande do Sul state bank. Thinner liquidity, a state-control discount, and a regionally concentrated book — the low multiple is often structural, not an obvious opportunity.
thesis.ABCB4: Mid-size wholesale bank. Neither a private giant’s umbrella nor a state bank’s political discount: the price follows the credit cycle and funding.
thesis.BMGB4: Focused on payroll loans and low-income retail. A low P/B usually tracks a high cost of capital and credit risk — looks like a banana, expensive if defaults widen.
thesis.BPAC11: Investment bank: revenue depends on issuance, M&A, and asset management. All of that reopens when the cost of capital falls.
thesis.VALE3: Dollar revenue from iron ore. China and FX explain far more of the stock price than any election poll.
thesis.GGBR4: Steel has a domestic leg (construction) and a U.S. leg. High rates here hurt, but U.S. results cushion local political risk.
thesis.WEGE3: Brazilian multinational selling motors and electrical equipment worldwide. The thesis is execution and the dollar, not Brasília.
thesis.EMBJ3: Dollar order book and defense exposure. Government matters as a customer and trade diplomacy, not as a controlling shareholder.
thesis.SUZB3: Pulp is a global dollar commodity. Historically a hedge: when political risk weakens the real, revenue rises in reais.
thesis.PRIO3: Oil without the state on the board. Useful to separate what in PETR4 is Brent from what is political risk.
thesis.TAEE11: Transmission with contracted, inflation-linked revenue. Competes directly with CDI: when Selic rises, the dividend looks less attractive and the stock falls.
thesis.VIVT3: Predictable, defensive cash flow. Political risk is regulatory (auctions, tariffs), not ownership control.
thesis.ABEV3: Staple consumption with low leverage. What moves it is household income and tax reform on beverages.
thesis.RADL3: Defensive retail: medicine gets bought in any scenario. Still hurt by high rates, because growth is worth less when discounted at 14%.
thesis.LREN3: Discretionary retail is the most sensitive gauge of rates and income. Often among the first to react when the yield curve opens or closes.
thesis.RENT3: Capital-intensive model funded by debt. Effectively a leveraged bet on the path of Selic.
